chief_complaint: dull frontal headache and hand swelling at 32 weeks gestation
hpi_details: 28F G1P0 at 32 weeks gestation presents for a routine prenatal visit. For the past 2 days, she has experienced a dull, persistent frontal headache. She also notes new-onset swelling in her hands, causing her rings to feel tight, and swelling in her feet. She denies visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, shortness of breath, or reduced fetal movements. Previous prenatal visits were uncomplicated with normal blood pressure readings. Today in clinic, her blood pressure is elevated at 148/96 mmHg and 150/98 mmHg on repeat, and urine dipstick shows 2+ protein.
ideas: patient thinks the hand and foot swelling and mild headache are just normal discomforts of the third trimester
concerns: patient is slightly worried because her rings became too tight to take off and the headache hasn't gone away
expectations: patient expects a routine check-up, to hear the baby's heartbeat, and receive reassurance
pmh: G1P0. No prior chronic medical history. Uncomplicated prenatal course until today; previous blood pressures have all been normal without proteinuria.
social_hx: Works as an office manager. Non-smoker, no alcohol or drug use during pregnancy.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Although edema is no longer part of the formal diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia due to its high prevalence in normal pregnancy, sudden non-dependent edema (hands, face) remains a significant clinical warning sign.

Preeclampsia can be diagnosed in the absence of proteinuria if new-onset hypertension is accompanied by new-onset end-organ dysfunction (e.g., thrombocytopenia, impaired liver function, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, or cerebral symptoms).
common_misconceptions: Dismissing a persistent headache in the third trimester as a normal symptom of pregnancy or tension headache, rather than a severe feature of preeclampsia.
Assuming that lower extremity edema is just normal dependent edema of pregnancy while ignoring the clinical significance of sudden upper extremity and facial swelling.
Waiting for blood pressure to reach severe ranges (>= 160/110 mmHg) before initiating a preeclampsia diagnostic workup.
Reassuring and discharging the patient from a routine visit without laboratory evaluation because she lacks right upper quadrant pain or visual changes.
core_concepts: Preeclampsia is diagnosed by new-onset hypertension (BP >= 140/90 mmHg) and proteinuria (dipstick 1+ or greater) after 20 weeks of gestation.
Headache, visual disturbances, and right upper quadrant pain are critical 'severe features' that indicate worsening disease and central nervous system or hepatic involvement.
Patients often present with non-specific symptoms such as swelling or headache at routine visits, requiring a high index of suspicion and active screening for preeclampsia.

Definitive management is delivery, but in preterm gestations (< 34 weeks), stabilization, fetal monitoring, and administration of corticosteroids for lung maturity are prioritized if maternal and fetal statuses permit.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize preeclampsia and inadvertently sending the symptomatic patient home without same-day hospital assessment.
Delaying comprehensive laboratory testing (CBC, platelets, LFTs, creatinine) and fetal monitoring (NST/BPP).
Overlooking the need for magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis if the patient's headache worsens or other severe features become apparent.
Omitting the administration of antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm delivery (< 34 weeks) becomes a clinical possibility.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dull frontal headache and hand swelling at 32 weeks gestation.
Key HPI features: persistent frontal headache for 2 days, new-onset rapid swelling of hands (rings tight) and feet in the third trimester.
Objective/Exam findings: Vitals show new-onset hypertension with BP 148/96 mmHg initially and 150/98 mmHg on repeat. Urine dipstick in clinic reveals 2+ proteinuria.
Relevant background/PMH: Previously normal blood pressure throughout the prenatal course.
management_principles: Recognize the condition during a routine prenatal visit and promptly transfer the patient to a labor and delivery triage unit for same-day assessment.
Perform a comprehensive stat laboratory workup including CBC, platelets, AST/ALT, creatinine, and a quantitative urine protein assessment (protein/creatinine ratio).
Initiate continuous fetal heart rate monitoring and ultrasonography to assess fetal status and amniotic fluid volume.
Administer antenatal corticosteroids (e.g., Betamethasone IM) for fetal lung maturity, as the patient is at 32 weeks gestation and may require preterm delivery.
Prepare to administer IV Magnesium Sulfate for seizure prophylaxis if severe features are confirmed, and use antihypertensives (IV Labetalol or Hydralazine) if blood pressure reaches severe ranges.

source_refs.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222: Gestational Hypertension and Preeclampsia

clinical_knowledge.topic: Preeclampsia with severe features evaluation and management

reference_soap.assessment: Preeclampsia at 32 weeks gestation. The presence of a persistent headache raises strong concern for preeclampsia with severe features, requiring urgent evaluation.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: BP 148/96 mmHg; repeat BP 15 minutes later 150/98 mmHg. HR 82, RR 18, Temp 37.0 C, SpO2 99% on room air. General: Well-appearing, in no acute distress. Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities to the shins; mild non-pitting edema noted in bilateral hands. Neuro: 2+ patellar reflexes bilaterally, no clonus. Fetal assessment: Fetal heart tones 145 bpm via Doppler, regular rhythm. Point-of-care Urine Dipstick: 2+ protein.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Same-day transfer to Labor & Delivery triage for comprehensive assessment. 2. Stat laboratory evaluation: CBC, platelets, AST, ALT, comprehensive metabolic panel (creatinine), and spot urine protein/creatinine ratio. 3. Initiate continuous external fetal monitoring (NST) and perform an ultrasound for fetal growth and amniotic fluid index. 4. Administer a course of IM Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity given the gestational age of 32 weeks and the potential need for preterm delivery. 5. Monitor closely; if severe features are definitively confirmed (e.g., worsening neurological symptoms, abnormal labs) or if BP worsens to severe range (>= 160/110 mmHg), initiate IV Magnesium Sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and appropriate antihypertensive therapy.
reference_soap.subjective: Chief Complaint: dull frontal headache and hand swelling at 32 weeks gestation  28F G1P0 at 32 weeks gestation presenting for a routine prenatal visit. Reports a dull, persistent frontal headache for the past 2 days that has not improved with rest. She also notes new, rapid swelling in her hands (her rings feel uncomfortably tight) and feet. Denies visual changes (no blurry vision or flashing lights), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, shortness of breath, nausea, or vomiting. Reports normal active fetal movements. Her prior prenatal visits have been uncomplicated with normal blood pressures and no prior proteinuria.

learning_objectives: Recognize the clinical presentation of preeclampsia during a routine prenatal visit, identifying key red flags such as new-onset headache and rapid upper-extremity edema.
Demonstrate the ability to systematically screen a pregnant patient with elevated blood pressure for severe features of preeclampsia (visual changes, epigastric pain, dyspnea).
Formulate an urgent, same-day diagnostic and triage plan for suspected preeclampsia, including essential maternal laboratory testing and fetal monitoring.
Understand the pharmacological management principles for preterm preeclampsia, including the indications for antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulfate, and antihypertensives.

must_ask.objective: Screen for visual symptoms of severe preeclampsia
must_ask.say: Have you noticed any blurry vision, flashing lights, or blind spots?

must_ask.objective: Screen for epigastric or right upper quadrant pain
must_ask.say: Are you having any pain under your ribs on the right side or in your upper stomach?
Have you felt any shortness of breath or difficulty breathing?
Have you noticed any changes in the baby's movements or kicking?

must_ask.objective: Clarify the persistence and relief of the headache
must_ask.say: Does the headache go away when you take medicine or rest?

must_ask.objective: Check baseline blood pressure from previous visits
must_ask.say: Has your blood pressure been normal at all of your previous prenatal visits?

teaching.one_liner: 28-year-old G1P0 at 32 weeks gestation presenting to clinic with new-onset hypertension, proteinuria, and a persistent frontal headache alongside sudden hand swelling.
red_flags: New-onset persistent headache in the third trimester
Sudden swelling of the hands or face

history.answer: I'm here for my regular thirty-two-week prenatal checkup, but over the past two days I've had this dull headache across my forehead and my rings have gotten really tight.
My last menstrual period started exactly thirty-two weeks ago, and my cycle has always been regular every twenty-eight days. The early ultrasound matched my dates perfectly.
Yes, my husband and I planned this pregnancy, and we're very excited, though I feel a little anxious today about this swelling and headache.
I had typical morning sickness during the first three months, but it completely resolved and I haven't had any nausea or vomiting recently.
No, I have not had any vaginal bleeding, spotting, or pelvic cramping at all.
It began two days ago as a dull, constant ache across my forehead. Resting in a dark room didn't help, and it has stayed about the same since it started.
No, my vision is completely normal, with no blurriness, double vision, dark spots, or flashes of light.
No, I have no pain under my ribs on the right side, no stomach burning, and no heartburn.

history.answer: About two days ago my hands became noticeably puffy, and my wedding ring got so tight that I couldn't slide it off. My feet and ankles are also more swollen than usual.
No, I haven't had any shortness of breath, chest tightness, or trouble breathing when lying flat.
I first felt quickening around nineteen weeks, and the baby has been kicking actively and normally today.
No, I haven't noticed any fluid leaking or gushing from my vagina, and I haven't felt any uterine tightening or rhythmic contractions.
At all my previous checkups my blood pressure was always normal, usually around 110 over 70.
This is my very first pregnancy. I have never been pregnant before and have never had a miscarriage or termination.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions, and I've never been told I had high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid trouble, or kidney disease.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take a daily prenatal vitamin containing folic acid. I took a regular Tylenol yesterday for the headache, but it didn't relieve it.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes, and I haven't touched any alcohol since learning I was pregnant.
I don't use any recreational drugs. I work in an office, so I'm not exposed to toxic chemicals, radiation, or sick patients.
I avoid raw meat, don't handle cat litter, and my early blood tests showed I am immune to rubella and negative for hepatitis B.
No, I haven't had any burning or pain with urination, and I don't have any unusual, itchy, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge.
My mother developed mild high blood pressure in her fifties, but there is no family history of preeclampsia, kidney disease, or birth defects.
I weighed sixty kilograms before getting pregnant and have gained about ten kilograms so far. I eat balanced meals and only have one cup of decaf tea a day.
My mood has been steady, and I feel completely safe at home with my husband, who is very supportive.
I work as an office manager at an accounting firm and live with my husband in an apartment.
I assumed the swelling and headache were just ordinary third-trimester aches, but I'm worried because the headache won't fade and my rings won't budge.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 148/96 mmHg, pulse 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-appearing woman in no acute distress, alert and oriented, with mild puffiness around the eyes and face.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, and funduscopic examination shows sharp optic disc margins with no papilledema or arteriolar narrowing.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation without crackles, rales, or wheezing.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds and no audible murmurs or gallops.
Gravid abdomen consistent with a third-trimester pregnancy, without distension or surgical scars.
Symphysis-fundal height measures 32 centimeters, uterus is soft and non-tender, and there is no tenderness in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium.
Fetal heart tones are clearly audible via Doppler at 145 beats per minute with a regular rhythm in the lower quadrant.
Two-plus pitting edema over bilateral lower extremities extending up to the mid-shins, along with mild non-pitting edema of bilateral hands.
Bilateral patellar deep tendon reflexes are two-plus, and rapid dorsiflexion of both ankles reveals no clonus.
